title: Write from scratch, zero-shot
summary: Writing every weight in one reply with no tools or rollouts, Opus 5.5's median network beat PPO-100k on 4/5 environments (CartPole, MountainCar, LunarLander, Breakout; H1 needs ≥ 4) and its best network matched or beat the final PPO checkpoint on 3/5 (CartPole, MountainCar, Breakout; median: 2/5). Total API cost $6.85.

table.caption: Mean return over 100 seeded greedy episodes (success rate in parentheses: CartPole 500 steps, Acrobot goal, MountainCar flag, LunarLander return ≥ 200). Heuristic agreement = share of visited steps where the network's action equals a hand-coded controller's (MountainCar: push with velocity; LunarLander: Gymnasium heuristic(); CartPole/Acrobot: secondary reference rules).

runs.label: CartPole · attempt 1
runs.answer: Bang-bang linear state feedback: s = 1.0·x + 1.7·ẋ + 19·θ + 3.5·θ̇. Push right (action 1) if s > 0, else push left (action 0). The gains are LQR-like, so the pole is balanced and the cart is pulled back toward the centre.
runs.reasoning_excerpt:
CONTROLLER: Bang-bang linear state feedback: s = 1.0·x + 1.7·ẋ + 19·θ + 3.5·θ̇. Push right (action 1) if s > 0, else push left (action 0). The gains are LQR-like, so the pole is balanced and the cart is pulled back toward the centre.

**How the network works**

- **Layer 1, unit 0:** computes h1₀ = tanh(1.0·x + 1.7·ẋ + 19·θ + 3.5·θ̇). Tanh is odd and monotonic, so the sign of h1₀ equals the sign of s. All other units are 0.
- **Layer 2, unit 0:** computes h2₀ = tanh(h1₀), which keeps the same sign. All other units are tanh(0) = 0.
- **Output:** logit₀ = 0 and logit₁ = h2₀. Argmax picks action 1 (push right) when s > 0 and action 0 (push left) otherwise. An exact tie goes to action 0, which does not matter.

**Why these signs and gains**

- **Angle terms:** pushing right gives a negative angular acceleration. So when the pole leans right (θ > 0) or is rotating right (θ̇ > 0), we push right.
- **Cart terms:** the cart-position and cart-velocity gains are also positive, as in the standard LQR solution for an inverted pendulum on a cart. The controller first pushes the cart further out so the pole tilts back toward the centre, then the angle terms drive the cart home. This stops the cart drifting past ±2.4 during the 500 steps.
- **Gain size:** the gains match LQR with Q = I and R = 1 for these parameters, roughly K ≈ [1, 1.6, 19, 3.4]. Under bang-bang actuation, one step changes θ̇ by about 0.29 rad/s and ẋ by about 0.2 m/s. That gives small chattering, around 0.006 rad in angle

runs.label: CartPole · attempt 2
runs.answer: Bang-bang linear state feedback: push right (action 1) if 0.5·x + 1.0·x_dot + 10·θ + 2·θ_dot > 0, otherwise push left (action 0). This is an LQR-style gain ratio, with all gains having the same sign.
runs.reasoning_excerpt:
CONTROLLER: Bang-bang linear state feedback: push right (action 1) if 0.5·x + 1.0·x_dot + 10·θ + 2·θ_dot > 0, otherwise push left (action 0). This is an LQR-style gain ratio, with all gains having the same sign.

**Why this controller**

In this environment's sign convention, a positive force (push right) produces negative angular acceleration of the pole. So a pole leaning right (θ>0) or falling right (θ_dot>0) is corrected by pushing right.

The cart-position terms also take a positive sign, which may look backwards. To return a cart sitting at x>0 to the centre, the pole must first be tipped left, and that requires a brief push to the right. This "non-minimum-phase" structure is why LQR solutions for the cart-pole have all four gains with the same sign.

**How the gains were chosen**

Typical LQR gain ratios for this system are roughly x : x_dot : θ : θ_dot ≈ 1 : 1.6 : 18 : 3. I used s = 0.5x + 1.0x_dot + 10θ + 2θ_dot. This is θ + 0.2θ_dot + 0.05x + 0.1x_dot, scaled by 10.
- The angle and angular-velocity terms dominate, which keeps the pole upright.
- The small cart terms counteract slow drift of the cart over 500 steps.

These gains come from reasoning only; I could not run any test episodes.

**How the network implements it**

- **Hidden unit 1, layer 1:** h1₀ = tanh(s), using the four input weights above and zero bias. Because tanh is monotonic, it preserves the sign of s even when it saturates.
- **Hidden unit 1, layer 2:** h2₀ = tanh(h1₀) also preserves the sign.

runs.label: Acrobot · attempt 2
runs.answer: Bang-bang energy pumping: torque = +1 if dθ1 + 0.25·dθ2 > 0, else −1. Torque follows link 1's swing direction, which pumps the in-phase swing mode, damps the out-of-phase mode, and avoids runaway spinning of link 2.
runs.reasoning_excerpt:
CONTROLLER: Bang-bang energy pumping: torque = +1 if dθ1 + 0.25·dθ2 > 0, else −1. Torque follows link 1's swing direction, which pumps the in-phase swing mode, damps the out-of-phase mode, and avoids runaway spinning of link 2.

**Why this controller**

- **How energy enters the system.** The actuator works only through the joint angle, so the energy input rate is τ·dθ2. The target height needs about 24.5 J above the hanging state; the cheapest goal configuration is link 1 horizontal with link 2 pointing up.
- **Two swing modes near the bottom.** Linearising the given dynamics (d1 = 4.5, d2 = 1.75, m22 = 1.25, gravity stiffness [[19.6, 4.9], [4.9, 4.9]]) gives:
  - a slow in-phase mode, ω ≈ 1.88 rad/s, with θ2 ≈ +2.8·θ1;
  - a fast out-of-phase mode, ω ≈ 2.82 rad/s, with θ2 ≈ −1.8·θ1.
- **Why pump the in-phase mode.** In that mode link 2 swings much higher than link 1, which is what raises the tip.
- **Why sign(dθ1) does this.** Torque = sign(dθ1) gives positive power (dθ2 has the same sign as dθ1) in the in-phase mode. It gives negative power in the out-of-phase mode, so that mode is damped.
- **Why not sign(dθ2).** Pure sign(dθ2) pumping would add energy faster, but mostly into the out-of-phase mode. It also risks link 2 spinning continuously, which can stall the swing-up.
- **The small dθ2 term.** Adding 0.25·dθ2 recovers positive power near the turning points of link 1, where |dθ1| is small but |dθ2| is large. Since 0.25 < 0.56, the out-of-phase mode is still damped.

runs.label: Acrobot · attempt 3
runs.answer: Bang-bang energy pumping on the slow "swing" mode: torque = +1 if (dθ1 + 0.4·dθ2) > 0, else -1 (zero torque is never used).
runs.reasoning_excerpt:
CONTROLLER: Bang-bang energy pumping on the slow "swing" mode: torque = +1 if (dθ1 + 0.4·dθ2) > 0, else -1 (zero torque is never used).

**Why this rule**

Linearise the acrobot about the hanging position:
- Mass matrix M = [[4.5, 1.75], [1.75, 1.25]].
- Gravity stiffness K = g·[[2, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5]].

This gives two oscillation modes:
- **Slow "swing" mode** (ω ≈ 1.88 rad/s): θ2 ≈ 2.8·θ1, so link 2 swings with link 1 and even further. This is the mode that lifts the tip, because link 2 can flip upward while link 1 is high.
- **Fast "jackknife" mode** (ω ≈ 2.82 rad/s): θ2 ≈ -1.79·θ1, so the links fold against each other. The tip barely rises in this mode, so energy put here is mostly wasted.

The power the motor delivers is τ·dθ2. In modal coordinates this power goes to:
- the swing mode in proportion to τ·(dθ1 + 0.56·dθ2);
- the jackknife mode in proportion to −τ·(dθ1 − 0.56·dθ2), i.e. with the opposite sign.

So with τ = sign(dθ1 + c·dθ2):
- For any c ≥ 0, the swing mode is resonantly pumped. This is the bang-bang version of Spong's swing-up rule, which bends link 2 in the direction link 1 is moving.
- For c < 0.56, the jackknife mode is mildly damped rather than pumped.
- c = 0.4 is a hedge for the nonlinear phase. If link 2 whirls fast (|dθ2| ≫ |dθ1|), the rule reduces to sign(dθ2), which is the greedy energy-maximising torque. This keeps energy from stalling, so the episode should not hit the -500 cap.

runs.label: MountainCar · attempt 1
runs.answer: Bang-bang energy pumping: push right (action 2) when velocity > 0, push left (action 0) when velocity < 0. At velocity exactly 0 (the reset state) the logits tie and the argmax picks left, so every episode starts by swinging left.
runs.reasoning_excerpt:
CONTROLLER: Bang-bang energy pumping: push right (action 2) when velocity > 0, push left (action 0) when velocity < 0. At velocity exactly 0 (the reset state) the logits tie and the argmax picks left, so every episode starts by swinging left.

**How the network works**

- **Layer 1:** unit 0 computes h1[0] = tanh(1000·velocity). This is roughly the sign of the velocity, and it keeps the correct sign even for very small velocities. The position input is unused.
- **Layer 2:** unit 0 computes h2[0] = tanh(10·h1[0]). This sharpens the sign further.
- **Output:** the logits are (−h2[0], 0, +h2[0]).
  - When velocity > 0, action 2 (accelerate right) has the largest logit.
  - When velocity < 0, action 0 (accelerate left) has the largest logit.
  - When velocity = 0 (at reset, or after hitting the left wall), all logits are 0. The tie goes to the lowest index, so the action is left.
- **Unused units:** all other units have zero weights and zero biases. Their activations are 0, so they contribute nothing.

**Why this controller should work**

- Pushing in the direction of motion adds the maximum possible mechanical energy at every step. The oscillation amplitude grows as fast as the force allows, until the car clears the right hill.
- The first action pushes left. That builds a swing up the left hill, followed by a powerful run to the right. From every start in [−0.6, −0.4], this should reach the flag in roughly 1.5 swings, well inside the 200-step limit.

  - At the start (v = 0), the sign depends only on whether x0 is left or right of −0.485.
- **Layer 2, unit 0:** h2 = tanh(10·h1). This keeps the sign and saturates the value.
- **Outputs:** the logits are [−h2, −1, +h2]. So the action is right (2) when h2 > 0 and left (0) when h2 < 0. The no-op logit is fixed at −1, so no-op is never chosen.

runs.answer: Gymnasium's heuristic lander. angle_targ=clip(0.5x+vx,±0.4); hover_targ=0.55|x|; angle_todo=0.5(angle_targ-θ)-ω; hover_todo=0.5(hover_targ-y)-0.5vy. Main engine if hover_todo>|angle_todo| and >0.05; else right if angle_todo<-0.05; else left if >0.05. On leg contact: main only if vy<-0.1.
runs.reasoning_excerpt:
CONTROLLER: Gymnasium's heuristic lander. angle_targ=clip(0.5x+vx,±0.4); hover_targ=0.55|x|; angle_todo=0.5(angle_targ-θ)-ω; hover_todo=0.5(hover_targ-y)-0.5vy. Main engine if hover_todo>|angle_todo| and >0.05; else right if angle_todo<-0.05; else left if >0.05. On leg contact: main only if vy<-0.1.

**How the network implements it**

The network has three stages: layer 1 builds the features, layer 2 makes the threshold decisions, and layer 3 combines them. I reasoned this out without running it, so the weights are untested.

**Layer 1 (feature units)**

Most units use small gains so that tanh stays nearly linear. A few use large gains on purpose, to produce a clip, a step, or a gate.

- **h0** = tanh(2.5·(0.5x + vx)). Then 0.4·h0 is a soft version of the clipped angle target.
- **h1** = tanh(0.2·(−0.5θ − ω)). Then 5·h1 ≈ −0.5θ − ω, the linear part of angle_todo.
- **h2** = tanh(0.2·(−0.5y − 0.5vy)). Then 5·h2 ≈ the linear part of hover_todo.
